source.title: Efficiently Attacking Memorization Scores
source.authors: Tue Do; Varun Chandrasekaran; Daniel Alabi

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies attacks to training data and reports test accuracy after those interventions, an attack setting that bears on generalization but does not test a listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports that test accuracy does not change significantly after its attacks on a small fraction of training data. Its memorization-score results measure score manipulation, not the claim versions’ generalization findings.
record.test_reason: The study uses label-memorization scores and proxies to evaluate adversarial score manipulation. Neither its score results nor its test-accuracy checks test V1–V8. In particular, it modifies randomly selected inputs rather than removing highly memorized examples and comparing retraining accuracy with matched random removals as V8 requires.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that scaled pseudoinverse transformations produce images with high memorization scores and demonstrate vulnerabilities in memorization scores and proxies. They also present a theoretical framework for score manipulation. They do not establish or refute the removal-and-retraining result in V8.
record.recipe_differences: The study attacks memorization-score estimators by modifying input data; it does not reproduce the original generalization experiments or interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack size and architecture affect the relative attack-score advantage; PINV loses its advantage in some settings at attack size 104. Test accuracy is reported for CIFAR10 across three architectures and attack-set sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors characterize CIFAR-10 test-accuracy changes after attacks on 10, 100 or 1000 inputs as negligible across VGG-11, ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Manipulating a small fraction of training inputs to attack memorization scores can leave held-out accuracy largely unchanged in these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 3–5 report that deliberately applying PINV increases label-memorization scores across the three datasets and convolutional architectures; other experiments report manipulation of score proxies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-memorization scores and their proxies are vulnerable to targeted input manipulation.

record.problems: The test-accuracy check is limited to CIFAR10 and three architectures; attacks alter a small fraction of the training set (at most 2%). The paper describes changes as not significant but Table 16 gives means and variances without a significance test. Main experiments use five trials; label-memorization scoring uses n = 100 models per scoring run.
record.rows_left_out: None; Table 16 results are recorded for all three models, four attacks and three attack-set sizes, with corresponding no-attack reference rows.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance random-label test accuracy.
Test-error changes when width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-scaled weight sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing measures. Input-loss curvature used here is a different construct.
Retraining after removing the most memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples; no such removal experiment is reported.

record.verdict_notes: All row values and baselines match Table 16 except r40. The table reports results over five trials and describes its uncertainty as variance; no formal significance test is supplied. The authors' negligible-change characterization concerns attack effects, not absence of any V1–V8 effect. Raising self-influence scores while retaining most training data does not test the accuracy cost of removing highly memorized examples.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Whether magnitude-aware sharpness tracks the train-test gap.
Removing highly memorized examples and comparing test accuracy with random removals.
